items.rationale: Column i is the endpoint's linear and angular velocity produced by a unit rate at joint i alone, with every other joint held still. Option a describes the sum of all columns, and b is the 'differentiate the pose' view the learner tends to fall back on.

Column 1 linear part is z0 × (O2 − O0) = (0,0,1) × (1,1,0) = (−1, 1, 0), so the y-component is 1 m/s. Using the arm from joint 2 to the tip, (0,1,0), gives y = 0 (wrong moment arm). Using r × z gives −1 (wrong order and sign).

A prismatic joint translates the whole endpoint along its axis at unit speed and rotates nothing: column = [z1; 0]. Options b and d carry the rotary cross product over to a prismatic joint, and b also gives it a nonzero angular part.

Joint 2 rotates about its own axis z1, which turning joint 2 does not change; only joints before it (here θ1) can reorient that axis. So the angular part of column i depends on the earlier joints, not on joint i. This is the 'column i depends on θi alone' surprise, and the off-by-one trap from M3, in a different form.
The moment arm gets longer, so z × r changes and the linear part changes. The angular part is just the joint axis direction, which does not depend on which point you track.

accepted: along the length of the arm
items.rationale: Column 1 is (0,2) and column 2 is (0,1) in the (x, y) plane, since each is z × (arm vector) and the arm vector lies along x. Both columns point along y, so no joint rates move the tip along x (a singularity, with the arm fully stretched).
